lesson.title: An Empire of Liberty: The Birth of Manifest Destiny
lesson.summary: Manifest Destiny was the widely held nineteenth century belief that the United States was fated to spread across North America, turning earlier exploration and postwar national pride into a program for continental expansion.
lesson.body:
The phrase itself came from a journalist. In the summer of 1845, John L. O'Sullivan wrote in the United States Magazine and Democratic Review that it was America's "manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence." O'Sullivan was arguing for the annexation of Texas, but the idea he named was already decades old. He simply gave a slogan to a set of beliefs that had been building since the early republic: that the United States was not just one nation among many, but a special experiment in liberty that was meant to keep growing.

Part of that confidence came from the Era of Good Feelings. After the War of 1812 ended in 1815, the collapse of the Federalist Party left James Monroe's Republicans without serious opposition, and the country enjoyed a rare stretch of political unity from roughly 1817 to 1825. Monroe's administration asserted American interests hemisphere wide with the Monroe Doctrine in 1823, warning European powers against further colonization in the Americas. That mix of unity and assertiveness taught a generation of Americans to think of their country as a rising power with a right to shape the continent around it.

Confidence needed a map, and that came from the Lewis and Clark Expedition. After Thomas Jefferson bought the Louisiana Territory from France in 1803, he sent Meriwether Lewis and William Clark to explore it, and their journey from 1804 to 1806 carried them up the Missouri River, over the Rocky Mountains, and down to the Pacific Ocean. Their reports on rivers, soil, and native nations turned the West from a rumor into a place that could be settled, farmed, and governed. Fur traders, missionaries, and land speculators followed the trails the expedition had charted, and the vague hope of a continental nation became a concrete, achievable plan.

Manifest Destiny was never just geography. It rested on the idea that Providence favored American institutions, on Jefferson's vision of a republic of independent farmers who needed endless new land, and on a racial hierarchy that dismissed Native American and Mexican claims to the land as temporary obstacles rather than legitimate rights. Economic motives mattered too: access to Pacific ports, fertile farmland, and mineral wealth. These strands wove together into a conviction that expansion was not just desirable but destined, which made it easier to justify displacing the people already living on the land.

The consequences followed quickly. The belief helped justify the forced removal of Native nations in the 1830s, including the Cherokee Trail of Tears, and it fed directly into the annexation of Texas in 1845 and the settlement of the Oregon boundary with Britain in 1846. It also pushed the United States toward war with Mexico. Not everyone cheered. Whigs in Congress and early abolitionists warned that Manifest Destiny was becoming a convenient cover for extending slavery into new territory, a fear that would prove well founded as the nation pressed further west.
